name: Dexfenfluramine (Redux)

lead: Dexfenfluramine (Redux) was an appetite-suppressing drug approved in the US in the mid-1990s for obesity. Trials showed weight loss with diet, and it was widely prescribed, including with phentermine as fen-phen.
It was withdrawn in September 1997 after valve disease and pulmonary hypertension were reported in users. It is not available today.

paras: It raises serotonin signalling in the brain by releasing serotonin and blocking its reuptake, which reduces appetite. Its metabolite also activates 5-HT2B receptors, which researchers link to the heart and lung harms.
Documented harms include heart-valve disease and pulmonary hypertension, which led to withdrawal. It is not marketed anywhere reported in the sources and is not a legitimate option today.

Multiple Doses of DM199 in Patients With Chronic Kidney Disease (REDUX)

lead: Dexfenfluramine, sold in the United States under the brand name Redux, is the dextrorotatory enantiomer of fenfluramine and was developed as a serotonin-acting appetite suppressant for obesity. It is structurally related to amphetamine but is described as lacking amphetamine-type stimulant effects.[1][2]

Interneuron Pharmaceuticals, co-founded by MIT researcher Richard Wurtman, developed the drug and licensed its patent to Wyeth-Ayerst Laboratories. The FDA approved it for weight loss in the mid-1990s, and approval was withdrawn in September 1997 after reports of cardiovascular harm, chiefly heart-valve disease and pulmonary hypertension.[1][3]

Controlled trials from the 1980s and 1990s examined long-term dexfenfluramine treatment in obesity,[4] and later pharmacology work linked the drug's cardiac and pulmonary harms to activation of the serotonin 5-HT2B receptor by its active metabolite.[3][5] It is no longer marketed, and it appears in appearance-focused discussion mainly as a historical diet drug and as half of the "fen-phen" combination.
infobox: Withdrawn; unscheduled in the US; Brazil lists it as prohibited

paras: Dexfenfluramine was approved as an adjunct to diet and exercise for obesity in adults. Its only recognised use was weight reduction through reduced appetite.[1][6]

The Lancet published an international trial of long-term dexfenfluramine in obesity in 1989,[4] and reviews of serotonergic agents describe sustained serotonin signalling in the hypothalamus as a basis for appetite control, with 5-HT2C and 5-HT1B receptors implicated.[6] Reviews also note that serotonin-acting drugs of this kind produced clinically meaningful weight loss over a year or longer.[6]

A set of 1998 studies in the New England Journal of Medicine then examined heart-valve findings in people who had taken appetite-suppressant drugs, including a placebo-controlled assessment of dexfenfluramine and sustained-release dexfenfluramine, and a population-based study of valve regurgitation.[7][8][9]

Separate research used a dexfenfluramine challenge together with PET imaging to investigate serotonin function in MDMA users (registered trial NCT01296802).[10] That work concerns serotonin neuroscience rather than weight loss.

The drug was withdrawn because of heart-valve disease and pulmonary hypertension. Pharmacological studies report that the valve changes resemble those seen in carcinoid disease or with some ergot drugs, and propose that 5-HT2B receptor stimulation on valve cells, by the drug's metabolite, drives the cell proliferation involved.[3]

A 2002 Nature Medicine study reported that dexfenfluramine increases pulmonary hypertension risk in humans and that its active metabolite is a selective 5-HT2B agonist; it found a role for this receptor in the disease process.[5]
Dexfenfluramine promotes release of serotonin and inhibits its reuptake, and its main metabolite is dexnorfenfluramine.[1][2] Its reported elimination half-life is roughly 17-20 hours.[1]

Twenty-two neurologists petitioned the FDA to delay approval, citing animal work on serotonin neuron damage whose methods and conclusions were later questioned.[1] After approval, reports of valve disease emerged, and the FDA announced the withdrawal on 15 September 1997; other markets followed.[1] Sibutramine later filled the niche and was itself removed from the US market in 2010.[1]

Redux was widely prescribed alone and alongside phentermine in the "fen-phen" regimen, according to Grokipedia, which also reports that more than 100 valve cases were recorded, some requiring surgery.[2] Those figures come from an AI-generated reference page and were not checked against primary sources.
